To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) habitual smartphone use is a key determinant for addictive smartphone behavior; (2) process and social usage are the most important predictors for both habitual and addictive smartphone usage; (3) emotional intelligence does not influence habitual and addictive smartphone use; (4) social stress is positively correlated with addictive smartphone use; and (5) self-regulation is negatively related with habitual and addictive smartphone behaviors; (6) men experience less social stresses and use their smartphones for less social purposes;

(1) habitual smartphone behavior has a positive effect on addictive smartphone behavior, (2) process related smartphone usage is positively related to addictive and habitual smartphone behavior, (3) social smartphone usage has a negative effect on addictive and habitual smartphone usage, (4) emotional intelligence has no influence on addictive smartphone behavior and habitual smartphone behavior.

habitual smartphone use and process and social smartphone use are important contributors to addictive smartphone behavior, whereas social stress positively influences the addictive smartphone behavior, a failure of selfregulation seems to cause higher risk of addictive addiction, women have a higher risk of developing addictive behavior, and older people are less likely to develop addictive behaviors.
